question: In a 35-year-old patient with ischaemic stroke, the aetiological workup should include tests for thrombophilia (e.g., antiphospholipid antibodies, protein C and S), arterial dissection imaging, and echocardiography, because these causes are disproportionately more common in young stroke compared to elderly patients.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Review the Diagnostic Workup in Young Stroke block. Young-stroke aetiology is fundamentally different: dissection, PFO, thrombophilia, and vasculitis must be systematically screened — these are commonly missed if the standard elderly-stroke workup alone is applied.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Young stroke (age < 45 years) requires an expanded workup. Arterial dissection, patent foramen ovale, antiphospholipid syndrome, and inherited thrombophilias are significantly more prevalent in this age group than in elderly patients where atherosclerosis and AF dominate.
